attachment.content:
- update-config: Use this skill to configure the Claude Code harness via settings.json. Automated behaviors ("from now on when X", "each time X", "whenever X", "before/after X") require hooks configured in settings.json - the harness executes these, not Claude, so memory/preferences cannot fulfill them. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.
- keybindings-help: Use when the user wants to customize keyboard shortcuts, rebind keys, add chord bindings, or modify ~/.claude/keybindings.json. Examples: "rebind ctrl+s", "add a chord shortcut", "change the submit key", "customize keybindings".
- simplify: Review changed code for reuse, quality, and efficiency, then fix any issues found.
- fewer-permission-prompts: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.
- loop: Run a prompt or slash command on a recurring interval (e.g. /loop 5m /foo). Omit the interval to let the model self-pace. - When the user wants to set up a recurring task, poll for status, or run something repeatedly on an interval (e.g. "check the deploy every 5 minutes", "keep running /babysit-prs"). Do NOT invoke for one-off tasks.
- schedule: Create, update, list, or run scheduled remote agents (routines) that execute on a cron schedule. - When the user wants to schedule a recurring remote agent, set up automated tasks, create a cron job for Claude Code, or manage their scheduled agents/routines. Also use when the user wants a one-time scheduled run ("run this once at 3pm", "remind me to check X tomorrow").
- claude-api: Build, debug, and optimize Claude API / Anthropic SDK apps. Apps built with this skill should include prompt caching. Also handles migrating existing Claude API code between Claude model versions (4.5 → 4.6, 4.6 → 4.7, retired-model replacements).
TRIGGER when: code imports `anthropic`/`@anthropic-ai/sdk`; user asks for the Claude API, Anthropic SDK, or Managed Agents; user adds/modifies/tunes a Claude feature (caching, thinking, compaction, tool use, batch, files, citations, memory) or model (Opus/Sonnet/Haiku) in a file; questions about prompt caching / cache hit rate in an Anthropic SDK project.
SKIP: file imports `openai`/other-provider SDK, filename like `*-openai.py`/`*-generic.py`, provider-neutral code, general programming/ML.
- init: Initialize a new CLAUDE.md file with codebase documentation
- review: Review a pull request
- security-review: Complete a security review of the pending changes on the current branch

Generation mode 是 depth estimation 的显著混淆变量。Methodology 段落阐述 continuation mode 作为 canonical condition 的选择及理由（不作为独立 claim）。

## Story Spine

- **Problem**: Web 数据正被多代递归合成文本污染。当前检测方法将合成文本视为 binary 类别（real vs synthetic），但质量随代际深度非线性退化——首代合成文本与四代合成文本的质量差异巨大却被忽视。
- **Existing approaches & gaps**: Binary detectors (DivEye, Min-K%++) 不区分代际；model collapse 文献 (Shumailov et al., Alemohammad et al. 2024, Dohmatob et al. 2024) 描述宏观现象但不提供检测工具；data selection methods (DSIR, D4, DoReMi) 做分布匹配但不估计递归深度；Drayson et al. (2025) 将 binary MGT detection 应用于 importance resampling 以防止 model collapse，是目前最接近的工作。然而这些方法均做二值判断，**不估计文本经历了多少轮递归生成，也不量化辨别能力的饱和边界。**
- **Our framing**: 将递归生成建模为 iterated lossy channel，从信息论（DPI）推导出 K* 的必然存在。K* 是首次系统测量的 operational quantity——它告诉数据策展者"在什么深度以下，depth-aware curation 比 binary detection 更有价值"。通过 8 条件实验矩阵（4 model-mode configurations + 4 decoding strategies）系统表征 K*，揭示其 universality：**K*=2 在所有测试条件下不变**，表明递归生成存在一个与具体模型架构和解码策略无关的 universal discrimination boundary。这一发现为数据治理提供 actionable guidance——depth-aware filtering 在 K* 以内有效，且无需针对不同模型或解码配置分别调优。
- **Headline result template**: "Recursive generation has a universal discrimination boundary at K*=2: invariant across 4 model-mode configurations and 4 decoding strategies (8 conditions total) at ≤1.5B scale, with cross-model transfer retention of 80-92% confirming depth features are largely text-intrinsic. Even this coarse 3-class signal yields X% improvement over binary filtering on MMLU/HellaSwag."

## Anticipated Reviewer Concerns & Responses

1. **"Universality claim 只基于 ≤1.5B 模型，能推广到更大模型吗？"** → 这是最大 limitation，论文明确标注 "at ≤1.5B scale"；但 (i) universality 在 4 个不同架构族（GPT-2 style, Pythia, OLMo, Qwen）间已成立，说明不是单一架构的 artifact；(ii) DPI 理论保证 K*_theory 对任意规模模型存在，实证 K*_empirical 在更大模型上可能更大（信号更丰富）也可能不变（lossy channel 特性稳定），这是重要的 future work
2. **"只是 feature engineering + off-the-shelf classifier，方法贡献弱"** → 贡献在 problem formulation + empirical characterization（首次测量 K*）+ 理论框架（DPI）+ universality 发现，不是分类器本身
3. **"Prompt-chain 不代表真实世界递归污染"** → retrain-chain ecological validity check 作为补充；prompt-chain 是 controlled experiment 的标准方法
4. **"K*=2 太浅，graduated filtering 收益有限"** → universality 恰好说明这是 fundamental boundary 而非实验 artifact；即使 K*=2，3-class（human/gen-1/gen-2+）比 binary 在阈值附近更 calibrated（exp-006）；K* 的 universality 意味着实践者无需为每个模型/解码配置单独标定阈值
5. **"同模型做生成和 surprisal 计算有 bias"** → **exp-013 直接反驳**：Pythia↔OLMo 90-92% accuracy retention，0v1 transfer AUC > 0.96。Depth signal 主要编码在文本而非 model self-familiarity
6. **"为什么不用 learned representations"** → 作为 baseline 对比；hand-crafted features 更 interpretable 且支持 degradation ordering 分析
7. **"Graduated filtering 没和 data selection methods 比"** → exp-006 包含 DSIR baseline + α sensitivity sweep
8. **"Decoding strategy 只测了 4 种，coverage 不够"** → 覆盖了实践中最常见的 decoding 配置（greedy, nucleus sampling, temperature scaling high/low）；4/4 完全一致强化 universality claim；extreme decoding（top-k=1 之外的 pathological 配置）留作 future work
9. **"为什么不直接用 LLM 做 depth estimation"** → **exp-011 直接反驳**：GPT-5.5 和 Claude Opus 4.6 在 500 样本 zero-shot 5-class depth 分类上仅 33.1-33.2% accuracy（MAE ~1.1），低于 OBD 15-feature LightGBM 的 38.6%。二者 binary detection 均 ~88%，说明 LLM 能区分 human vs synthetic 但无法估计递归深度。depth estimation 是非平凡任务，需要专用特征工程

## Venue Fit

- EMNLP 2026 special theme 明确呼吁 data contamination, synthetic data feedback loops, data governance 方向的工作
- 2+1 claim 结构：C1' 是 comprehensive characterization study with universality finding，C3 是 practical application，generation mode analysis 增加深度
- Universality narrative 比 controllability 更有 impact：从 "K* depends on X, Y, Z" 升级为 "K*=2 is a universal boundary"，审稿人更容易记住和传播
- 风险：universality claim 在 ≤1.5B 规模下的外推性是最大攻击面 → 论文中 scope 明确、limitation 诚实、DPI 理论支撑泛化的合理性

1	\section{Discussion}
2	\label{sec:discussion}
3	
4	\subsection{Theoretical Implications of $\Kempirical = 2$}
5	\label{sec:discuss_kstar}
6	
7	The Data Processing Inequality guarantees the existence of a finite $\Ktheory$ beyond which adjacent generations become indistinguishable (Section~\ref{sec:formulation}).
8	Our empirical result---$\Kempirical = 2$ uniformly across all 8 tested configurations (4 model-mode combinations from Section~\ref{sec:kstar_boundary} and 4 decoding strategies from the ablation)---establishes that this boundary is not only finite but remarkably shallow at the $\leq$1.5B parameter scale.
9	
10	The shallowness of $\Kempirical$ is explained by the rate of information loss across generations.
11	The 0v1 boundary is near-trivially separable ($\auc > 0.99$ across all configurations), reflecting the large distributional gap between human text and first-generation synthetic text.
12	At the 1v2 boundary, $\auc$ drops by approximately 30 percentage points ($\auc$ range: 0.6112--0.7039), indicating that the majority of the discriminative signal is consumed in the first generation step.
13	By the 2v3 boundary, $\auc$ falls to 0.5496--0.5917---below the operational threshold $\theta = 0.60$---and deeper pairs converge toward chance.
14	Recursive generation thus acts as a severely lossy channel whose information bottleneck is traversed within two steps.
15	
16	The feature degradation analysis (Section~\ref{sec:feature_degradation}) provides mechanistic evidence for this rapid collapse.
17	The most discriminative features---surprisal variance (\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std}) and its derivatives---all capture the heterogeneity of token-level predictability.
18	Human text exhibits high surprisal variance reflecting diverse syntactic structures and unpredictable discourse patterns.
19	The first generation step smooths this variance substantially, replacing high-surprisal tokens and atypical constructions with more predictable alternatives; the second step reduces the remaining variance to near-floor levels, leaving insufficient statistical fingerprint for reliable adjacent-depth discrimination.
20	Crucially, this degradation ordering is consistent across model families (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.85$ for all continuation-mode pairs), suggesting that the two-step information loss is governed by the autoregressive generation mechanism itself rather than by model-specific biases.
21	
22	This pattern aligns with findings from the model collapse literature.
23	Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} observed that tail-distribution degradation is most acute in the earliest generations, with minority modes vanishing before the output distribution stabilizes.
24	Dohmatob et al.~\cite{dohmatob2024model} derived scaling laws demonstrating that tail probability mass is lost at rates predictable from model and data scale.
25	Our $\Kempirical = 2$ provides a complementary, classifier-based measurement of this phenomenon: the information-theoretic discrimination boundary is reached after just two generation steps.
26	Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} proved convergence to a fixed point for self-consuming generative models; $\Kempirical = 2$ indicates that, operationally, the approach to this fixed point is rapid enough that adjacent-generation distinctions collapse within two steps.
27	
28	The invariance of $\Kempirical = 2$ across decoding strategies merits emphasis.
29	Greedy decoding, nucleus sampling ($p{=}0.9$), $T{=}0.7$, and $T{=}1.2$ all yield $\Kempirical = 2$, with 1v2 $\auc$ spanning a narrow range of [0.6866, 0.7039].
30	Higher decoding entropy modestly increases signal strength ($\auc_{1,2}$: 0.69 greedy $\to$ 0.70 at $T{=}1.2$) but does not shift the boundary.
31	This robustness suggests that $\Kempirical$ is governed by the fundamental information bottleneck of the generation process rather than by surface-level properties of the sampling algorithm.
32	
33	\subsection{Implications of Cross-Model Transfer}
34	\label{sec:discuss_transfer}
35	
36	The cross-model transfer results (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}) indicate that depth signals are largely encoded in text-level statistical properties rather than generator-specific artifacts.
37	Classifiers trained on Pythia-1.4B and evaluated on OLMo-1B retain 90--92\% of within-model accuracy, and the broader continuation-mode transfer matrix shows 80--92\% retention across all model pairs.
38	At the 0v1 boundary, cross-model $\auc$ exceeds 0.96 universally, confirming that binary contamination detection is fully transferable across generators.
39	
40	The practical implication is direct: a single depth classifier trained on one model's outputs can be deployed to estimate generational depth for texts produced by other models, without model-specific retraining.
41	This transferability extends the utility of depth estimation to open-web settings where the generating model is unknown---precisely the scenario where depth-aware data curation is most needed.
42	
43	Two caveats bound this conclusion.
44	First, the text-intrinsic component dominates, as evidenced by high cross-model transfer retention (80--92\% across continuation-mode pairs), yet a nontrivial model-specific residual persists.
45	The Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo pair, which spans different architectures and training corpora, achieves the highest cross-family retention (90--92\%), consistent with the depth signal being largely architecture-agnostic within continuation mode.
46	Second, Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$OLMo retention (80--85\%) is lower than Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo (90--92\%), indicating that model family similarity modulates transfer even among continuation-mode configurations.
47	
48	\subsection{Feature Importance Across Decoding Strategies}
49	\label{sec:discuss_features}
50	
51	While $\Kempirical = 2$ is invariant to decoding strategy (4/4 configurations), the feature importance ordering is not uniformly consistent.
52	Greedy decoding and $T{=}0.7$ share highly correlated feature rankings (Spearman $\rho = 0.914$), with top features dominated by vocabulary diversity measures: \texttt{self\_bleu}, \texttt{hapax\_ratio}, and \texttt{ttr}.
53	In contrast, greedy versus $T{=}1.2$ yields a lower correlation ($\rho = 0.53$, $p = 0.041$; suggestive but nonsignificant after Bonferroni correction for 6 pairwise comparisons), with $T{=}1.2$ promoting \texttt{hapax\_ratio}, \texttt{ttr}, and \texttt{surp\_skew} to the top ranks.
54	Notably, \texttt{freq\_entropy} rises from rank~10 under greedy ($\auc = 0.5139$) to rank~5 under $T{=}1.2$ ($\auc = 0.5905$), illustrating how high-entropy decoding amplifies frequency-distribution artifacts.
55	
56	This dissociation reveals an important distinction: the \emph{existence} of the depth boundary is robust, but the \emph{optimal feature subset} for detecting it depends on the sampling strategy.
57	High-entropy decoding amplifies frequency-distribution artifacts while attenuating vocabulary-diversity signals, shifting which text properties carry the most discriminative power without altering whether adjacent generations can be distinguished.
58	For practitioners, this implies that a universal depth classifier should incorporate features from multiple groups---surprisal moments, vocabulary diversity, and frequency tail statistics---to maintain performance across unknown decoding conditions.
59	
60	The cross-model feature ordering (Section~\ref{sec:feature_degradation}) provides a complementary perspective: among continuation-mode models, single-feature $\auc$ rankings are highly consistent (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.85$), with surprisal-variance features---\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std}, \texttt{surp\_d2\_std}---dominating uniformly.
61	A genuine limitation, however, is that depth-pair-level agreement weakens to $\tau \approx 0.37$ at the 1v2 boundary (Section~\ref{sec:feature_degradation}), indicating that the relative contribution of individual features at the discrimination boundary varies across models even when the aggregate ordering is shared.
62	
63	\subsection{LLM Zero-Shot Baseline}
64	\label{sec:discuss_llm}
65	
66	Frontier LLMs provide a natural baseline for depth estimation.
67	On a 500-sample test set with 5 depth classes (depths 0--4), GPT-5.5 achieves 33.2\% accuracy (MAE = 1.10) and Claude Opus~4.6 achieves 33.1\% accuracy (MAE = 1.15)---both below the OBD-LightGBM baseline of 38.6\% (MAE = 1.11).
68	Simultaneously, both models achieve approximately 88\% binary accuracy on the human-vs.-synthetic distinction (GPT-5.5: 87.8\%, Claude: 88.2\%).
69	
70	This gap between binary detection and depth estimation is informative.
71	Frontier LLMs can reliably determine \emph{whether} a text is machine-generated but cannot estimate \emph{how many generations of recursive processing} it has undergone.
72	Depth estimation requires sensitivity to subtle distributional shifts between adjacent generations---shifts orders of magnitude smaller than the human-vs.-machine gap.
73	The 15-dimensional statistical feature pipeline, despite its simplicity, captures these fine-grained shifts more effectively than frontier LLMs in a zero-shot setting.
74	This motivates the dedicated feature-engineering approach: the task demands specialized statistical sensitivity rather than general language understanding.
75	We evaluate only zero-shot prompting; few-shot or chain-of-thought strategies may narrow the gap and warrant future investigation.
76	
77	\subsection{Limitations}
78	\label{sec:limitations}
79	
80	We identify seven limitations that bound the generalizability of our findings.
81	
82	\emph{Model scale.}
83	All experiments use models at or below 1.5B parameters (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct).
84	Larger models may produce higher-fidelity text with weaker depth signatures, potentially shifting $\Kempirical$ beyond~2.
85	
86	\emph{Prompt-chain versus retrain-chain.}
87	Our recursive generation protocol is a prompt-chain: the same fixed model repeatedly generates from the previous output.
88	Real-world model collapse involves retrain-chains, where models are retrained on data from earlier generations~\cite{shumailov2024collapse}.
89	Retrain-chains introduce additional degradation through training dynamics, potentially producing different $\Kstar$ values.
90	
91	\emph{Language and domain.}
92	All experiments use English text from the C4 corpus.
93	Depth dynamics may differ across languages, domains (e.g., code, scientific text), and source corpora with different distributional properties.
94	
95	\emph{Decoding coverage.}
96	We test four decoding strategies (greedy, nucleus $p{=}0.9$, $T{=}0.7$, $T{=}1.2$).
97	Other strategies---top-$k$ sampling, beam search, contrastive decoding---remain untested and may yield different feature importance patterns or boundary behavior.
98	
99	\emph{Threshold sensitivity.}
100	$\Kempirical$ depends on the operational threshold $\theta$.
101	Sensitivity analysis across four decoding configurations shows $\Kempirical = 3$ at $\theta = 0.55$, $\Kempirical = 2$ for $\theta \in [0.60, 0.65]$, and $\Kempirical = 1$ at $\theta = 0.70$ (3 of 4 configurations).
102	The boundary is robust within a practical range but not invariant to threshold choice; our conclusions are conditioned on $\theta = 0.60$.
103	
104	\emph{Boundary marginality.}
105	The $\Kempirical = 2$ determination is statistically significant but numerically marginal at both ends.
106	On the lower side, Qwen-continuation's 1v2 CI lower bound (0.6015) exceeds $\theta = 0.60$ by only $+$0.15\,pp.
107	On the upper side, Qwen-rewrite's 2v3 CI upper bound (0.5991) falls below $\theta$ by only $-$0.09\,pp.
108	This narrow margin means that small changes in the feature set or classifier could shift the boundary.
109	Importantly, all eight boundary comparisons (four 1v2 and four 2v3) yield permutation $p < 0.01$, confirming that the statistical significance of the distinction is not in doubt---only its proximity to the operational threshold.
110	
111	\emph{Operational versus theoretical boundary.}
112	$\Kempirical$ is an operational lower bound that depends on the specific feature set and classifier.
113	$\Ktheory$ may be strictly greater; a more expressive classifier or richer feature representation could push $\Kempirical$ higher.
114	
115	\emph{Feature representation.}
116	The 15-dimensional hand-crafted feature set, while interpretable and transferable, is unlikely to be optimal.
117	Learned representations---fine-tuned embeddings or probing classifiers---may capture depth-discriminative patterns that statistical features miss, potentially achieving a higher $\Kempirical$.
118	
119	\paragraph{Graduated Filtering.}
120	% TODO: exp-006 graduated filtering 结果填充
121	
122	\subsection{Broader Impact}
123	\label{sec:broader_impact}
124	
125	The $\Kempirical = 2$ boundary has implications beyond the immediate scope of depth classification.
126	
127	\paragraph{Synthetic data curation.}
128	The practical consequence of $\Kempirical = 2$ is a three-tier taxonomy of text quality: human-authored (depth~0), first-generation synthetic (depth~1), and deeper synthetic (depth~$\geq 2$).
129	Texts at depth~$\geq 2$ are mutually indistinguishable and can be treated as a single category for curation purposes.
130	For practitioners filtering training data, this implies that a single round of synthetic rewriting suffices to make text statistically indistinguishable from text that has undergone multiple rounds of recycling---a form of one-wash laundering that limits the granularity of quality-based filtering.
131	This underscores the urgency of deploying depth-aware curation mechanisms before the first generation step, rather than relying on post-hoc detection.
132	Graduated filtering strategies that exploit this trichotomy may outperform binary human/synthetic filters, as the coarse ordinal signal (human / shallow / deep) captures the dominant axis of quality variation.
133	
134	\paragraph{Relation to model collapse.}
135	Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} and Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} study model collapse under \emph{retrain-chains}, where models are iteratively trained on their own outputs.
136	Our prompt-chain protocol measures an adjacent but distinct phenomenon: the degradation of statistical distinguishability under recursive generation by a fixed model.
137	The rapid convergence we observe ($\Kempirical = 2$) is consistent with the theoretical prediction of convergence to a fixed point, but the precise relationship between prompt-chain $\Kempirical$ and retrain-chain convergence rates remains an open question.
138	If prompt-chain depth signals serve as an observable proxy for early-stage model collapse, depth estimation could provide a lightweight diagnostic for data curation pipelines without requiring expensive retraining experiments.
139	
140	\paragraph{AI text detection.}
141	Current AI text detection is predominantly binary: human versus machine.
142	Our results suggest that \emph{depth-aware} detection provides a strictly more informative signal.
143	The near-perfect 0v1 separability ($\auc > 0.99$) confirms that binary detection is reliable at this scale, but the 1v2 boundary ($\auc$: 0.61--0.70) reveals that first-generation text retains measurable statistical distance from deeper synthetic text.
144	This additional dimension---how many generations of processing a text has undergone---may prove valuable for provenance tracking and corpus quality assessment, where the binary human/AI label elides important distinctions between lightly and heavily recycled content.

Dohmatob et al.~\cite{dohmatob2024model} derived scaling laws demonstrating that tail probability mass is lost at rates predictable from model and data scale.
Our $\Kempirical = 2$ provides a complementary, classifier-based measurement of this phenomenon: the information-theoretic discrimination boundary is reached after just two generation steps.
Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} proved convergence to a fixed point for self-consuming generative models; $\Kempirical = 2$ indicates that, operationally, the approach to this fixed point is rapid enough that adjacent-generation distinctions collapse within two steps.

The invariance of $\Kempirical = 2$ across decoding strategies merits emphasis.
Greedy decoding, nucleus sampling ($p{=}0.9$), $T{=}0.7$, and $T{=}1.2$ all yield $\Kempirical = 2$, with 1v2 $\auc$ spanning a narrow range of [0.6866, 0.7039].
Higher decoding entropy modestly increases signal strength ($\auc_{1,2}$: 0.69 greedy $\to$ 0.70 at $T{=}1.2$) but does not shift the boundary.
This robustness suggests that $\Kempirical$ is governed by the fundamental information bottleneck of the generation process rather than by surface-level properties of the sampling algorithm.

\subsection{Implications of Cross-Model Transfer}
\label{sec:discuss_transfer}

The cross-model transfer results (Section~\ref{sec:transfer}) indicate that depth signals are largely encoded in text-level statistical properties rather than generator-specific artifacts.
Classifiers trained on Pythia-1.4B and evaluated on OLMo-1B retain 90--92\% of within-model accuracy, and the broader continuation-mode transfer matrix shows 80--92\% retention across all model pairs.
At the 0v1 boundary, cross-model $\auc$ exceeds 0.96 universally, confirming that binary contamination detection is fully transferable across generators.

The practical implication is direct: a single depth classifier trained on one model's outputs can be deployed to estimate generational depth for texts produced by other models, without model-specific retraining.
This transferability extends the utility of depth estimation to open-web settings where the generating model is unknown---precisely the scenario where depth-aware data curation is most needed.

Two caveats bound this conclusion.
First, the text-intrinsic component dominates, as evidenced by high cross-model transfer retention (80--92\% across continuation-mode pairs), yet a nontrivial model-specific residual persists.
The Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo pair, which spans different architectures and training corpora, achieves the highest cross-family retention (90--92\%), consistent with the depth signal being largely architecture-agnostic within continuation mode.
Second, Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$OLMo retention (80--85\%) is lower than Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo (90--92\%), indicating that model family similarity modulates transfer even among continuation-mode configurations.

\subsection{Feature Importance Across Decoding Strategies}
\label{sec:discuss_features}

While $\Kempirical = 2$ is invariant to decoding strategy (4/4 configurations), the feature importance ordering is not uniformly consistent.
Greedy decoding and $T{=}0.7$ share highly correlated feature rankings (Spearman $\rho = 0.914$), with top features dominated by vocabulary diversity measures: \texttt{self\_bleu}, \texttt{hapax\_ratio}, and \texttt{ttr}.
In contrast, greedy versus $T{=}1.2$ yields a lower correlation ($\rho = 0.53$, $p = 0.041$; suggestive but nonsignificant after Bonferroni correction for 6 pairwise comparisons), with $T{=}1.2$ promoting \texttt{hapax\_ratio}, \texttt{ttr}, and \texttt{surp\_skew} to the top ranks.
Notably, \texttt{freq\_entropy} rises from rank~10 under greedy ($\auc = 0.5139$) to rank~5 under $T{=}1.2$ ($\auc = 0.5905$), illustrating how high-entropy decoding amplifies frequency-distribution artifacts.

This dissociation reveals an important distinction: the \emph{existence} of the depth boundary is robust, but the \emph{optimal feature subset} for detecting it depends on the sampling strategy.
High-entropy decoding amplifies frequency-distribution artifacts while attenuating vocabulary-diversity signals, shifting which text properties carry the most discriminative power without altering whether adjacent generations can be distinguished.
For practitioners, this implies that a universal depth classifier should incorporate features from multiple groups---surprisal moments, vocabulary diversity, and frequency tail statistics---to maintain performance across unknown decoding conditions.

The cross-model feature ordering (Section~\ref{sec:feature_degradation}) provides a complementary perspective: among continuation-mode models, single-feature $\auc$ rankings are highly consistent (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.85$), with surprisal-variance features---\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std}, \texttt{surp\_d2\_std}---dominating uniformly.
A genuine limitation, however, is that depth-pair-level agreement weakens to $\tau \approx 0.37$ at the 1v2 boundary (Section~\ref{sec:feature_degradation}), indicating that the relative contribution of individual features at the discrimination boundary varies across models even when the aggregate ordering is shared.

\subsection{LLM Zero-Shot Baseline}
\label{sec:discuss_llm}

Frontier LLMs provide a natural baseline for depth estimation.
On a 500-sample test set with 5 depth classes (depths 0--4), GPT-5.5 achieves 33.2\% accuracy (MAE = 1.10) and Claude Opus~4.6 achieves 33.1\% accuracy (MAE = 1.15)---both below the OBD-LightGBM baseline of 38.6\% (MAE = 1.11).
Simultaneously, both models achieve approximately 88\% binary accuracy on the human-vs.-synthetic distinction (GPT-5.5: 87.8\%, Claude: 88.2\%).

This gap between binary detection and depth estimation is informative.
Frontier LLMs can reliably determine \emph{whether} a text is machine-generated but cannot estimate \emph{how many generations of recursive processing} it has undergone.
Depth estimation requires sensitivity to subtle distributional shifts between adjacent generations---shifts orders of magnitude smaller than the human-vs.-machine gap.
The 15-dimensional statistical feature pipeline, despite its simplicity, captures these fine-grained shifts more effectively than frontier LLMs in a zero-shot setting.
This motivates the dedicated feature-engineering approach: the task demands specialized statistical sensitivity rather than general language understanding.
We evaluate only zero-shot prompting; few-shot or chain-of-thought strategies may narrow the gap and warrant future investigation.

\subsection{Limitations}
\label{sec:limitations}

We identify seven limitations that bound the generalizability of our findings.

\emph{Model scale.}
All experiments use models at or below 1.5B parameters (Pythia-1.4B, OLMo-1B, Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct).
Larger models may produce higher-fidelity text with weaker depth signatures, potentially shifting $\Kempirical$ beyond~2.

\emph{Prompt-chain versus retrain-chain.}
Our recursive generation protocol is a prompt-chain: the same fixed model repeatedly generates from the previous output.
Real-world model collapse involves retrain-chains, where models are retrained on data from earlier generations~\cite{shumailov2024collapse}.
Retrain-chains introduce additional degradation through training dynamics, potentially producing different $\Kstar$ values.

\emph{Language and domain.}
All experiments use English text from the C4 corpus.
Depth dynamics may differ across languages, domains (e.g., code, scientific text), and source corpora with different distributional properties.

\emph{Decoding coverage.}
We test four decoding strategies (greedy, nucleus $p{=}0.9$, $T{=}0.7$, $T{=}1.2$).
Other strategies---top-$k$ sampling, beam search, contrastive decoding---remain untested and may yield different feature importance patterns or boundary behavior.

\emph{Threshold sensitivity.}
$\Kempirical$ depends on the operational threshold $\theta$.
Sensitivity analysis across four decoding configurations shows $\Kempirical = 3$ at $\theta = 0.55$, $\Kempirical = 2$ for $\theta \in [0.60, 0.65]$, and $\Kempirical = 1$ at $\theta = 0.70$ (3 of 4 configurations).
The boundary is robust within a practical range but not invariant to threshold choice; our conclusions are conditioned on $\theta = 0.60$.

\emph{Boundary marginality.}
The $\Kempirical = 2$ determination is statistically significant but numerically marginal at both ends.
On the lower side, Qwen-continuation's 1v2 CI lower bound (0.6015) exceeds $\theta = 0.60$ by only $+$0.15\,pp.
On the upper side, Qwen-rewrite's 2v3 CI upper bound (0.5991) falls below $\theta$ by only $-$0.09\,pp.
This narrow margin means that small changes in the feature set or classifier could shift the boundary.
Importantly, all eight boundary comparisons (four 1v2 and four 2v3) yield permutation $p < 0.01$, confirming that the statistical significance of the distinction is not in doubt---only its proximity to the operational threshold.

\emph{Operational versus theoretical boundary.}
$\Kempirical$ is an operational lower bound that depends on the specific feature set and classifier.
$\Ktheory$ may be strictly greater; a more expressive classifier or richer feature representation could push $\Kempirical$ higher.

\emph{Feature representation.}
The 15-dimensional hand-crafted feature set, while interpretable and transferable, is unlikely to be optimal.
Learned representations---fine-tuned embeddings or probing classifiers---may capture depth-discriminative patterns that statistical features miss, potentially achieving a higher $\Kempirical$.

\paragraph{Graduated Filtering.}

\subsection{Broader Impact}
\label{sec:broader_impact}

The $\Kempirical = 2$ boundary has implications beyond the immediate scope of depth classification.

\paragraph{Synthetic data curation.}
The practical consequence of $\Kempirical = 2$ is a three-tier taxonomy of text quality: human-authored (depth~0), first-generation synthetic (depth~1), and deeper synthetic (depth~$\geq 2$).
Texts at depth~$\geq 2$ are mutually indistinguishable and can be treated as a single category for curation purposes.
For practitioners filtering training data, this implies that a single round of synthetic rewriting suffices to make text statistically indistinguishable from text that has undergone multiple rounds of recycling---a form of one-wash laundering that limits the granularity of quality-based filtering.
This underscores the urgency of deploying depth-aware curation mechanisms before the first generation step, rather than relying on post-hoc detection.
Graduated filtering strategies that exploit this trichotomy may outperform binary human/synthetic filters, as the coarse ordinal signal (human / shallow / deep) captures the dominant axis of quality variation.

\paragraph{Relation to model collapse.}
Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} and Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} study model collapse under \emph{retrain-chains}, where models are iteratively trained on their own outputs.
Our prompt-chain protocol measures an adjacent but distinct phenomenon: the degradation of statistical distinguishability under recursive generation by a fixed model.
The rapid convergence we observe ($\Kempirical = 2$) is consistent with the theoretical prediction of convergence to a fixed point, but the precise relationship between prompt-chain $\Kempirical$ and retrain-chain convergence rates remains an open question.
If prompt-chain depth signals serve as an observable proxy for early-stage model collapse, depth estimation could provide a lightweight diagnostic for data curation pipelines without requiring expensive retraining experiments.

\paragraph{AI text detection.}
Current AI text detection is predominantly binary: human versus machine.
Our results suggest that \emph{depth-aware} detection provides a strictly more informative signal.
The near-perfect 0v1 separability ($\auc > 0.99$) confirms that binary detection is reliable at this scale, but the 1v2 boundary ($\auc$: 0.61--0.70) reveals that first-generation text retains measurable statistical distance from deeper synthetic text.
This additional dimension---how many generations of processing a text has undergone---may prove valuable for provenance tracking and corpus quality assessment, where the binary human/AI label elides important distinctions between lightly and heavily recycled content.

\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:introduction}

Web-scale text corpora are increasingly contaminated by synthetic content that has itself been generated from earlier synthetic content.
Each pass through a language model constitutes a lossy channel: first-generation synthetic text retains much of the information structure of its human-written source, but within just two or three generations the output is qualitatively different---tail modes vanish, lexical diversity contracts, and surprisal distributions flatten~\cite{shumailov2024collapse, dohmatob2024model}.
This recursive degradation is not merely a theoretical concern; as synthetic text proliferates on the open web, training corpora inevitably ingest documents at varying generational depths, amplifying the risk of model collapse in downstream systems.
Yet the dominant paradigm in synthetic text detection treats all machine-generated text identically: a document is classified as human or synthetic, with no regard for how many rounds of recursive generation it has undergone.
This binary framing discards the generational depth dimension entirely.

The gap cuts across three research communities.
Binary detection methods---including DivEye~\cite{basani2026diveye}, Min-K\%++~\cite{zhang2024minkpp}, and CoDeC~\cite{zawalski2026codec}---achieve strong human-versus-machine separation but produce no depth estimate.
The model collapse literature provides macro-level characterizations of recursive degradation: Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} demonstrated irreversible tail loss, Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} proved convergence to a fixed point, and Schaeffer et al.~\cite{schaeffer2025position} organized the field into a taxonomy of eight definitions---yet none of these works provides a tool for estimating the generational depth of an individual text.
Data selection methods such as DSIR~\cite{xie2023dsir}, D4~\cite{tirumala2024d4}, and DoReMi~\cite{xie2024doremi} perform distribution matching to improve corpus quality but ignore recursive depth altogether.
The closest prior work is Drayson et al.~\cite{drayson2025}, who combined binary machine-generated text detection with stratified importance resampling to prevent model collapse---but their approach remains fundamentally binary.
No existing method estimates how many rounds of recursive generation a text has undergone, nor quantifies the boundary beyond which such estimation becomes infeasible.

Recursive generation forms an iterated lossy channel; the Data Processing Inequality guarantees that the original signal degrades monotonically across generations, motivating the existence of a finite discrimination boundary $\Kstar$ beyond which adjacent generations become indistinguishable.
Markov chain convergence further implies that adjacent-generation distributions converge to a shared stationary distribution, so the classifier's task grows harder with each step.
Motivated by this theoretical structure, we set out to empirically measure $\Kempirical$---the maximum depth at which a classifier can reliably distinguish adjacent generations.
Our approach combines a 15-dimensional statistical feature pipeline---capturing surprisal moments, surprisal derivatives, vocabulary diversity, and frequency tail statistics---with an Ordinal Binary Decomposition (OBD) LightGBM classifier that respects the ordinal structure of depth.
We operationalize $\Kempirical$ as the deepest generation at which adjacent depths remain statistically distinguishable, with the bootstrap 95\% CI for pairwise $\auc$ exceeding an operational threshold $\theta = 0.60$ (formal definition in Section~\ref{sec:method}).
The choice of interpretable statistical features---rather than learned representations---is deliberate: it enables cross-generator transfer without retraining and permits attribution of discriminative power to specific text properties.

Our contributions are organized into two groups.
The primary contribution is a systematic empirical characterization of $\Kempirical$ and its properties:

\begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*)]
  \item \textbf{$\Kempirical = 2$: a consistent boundary across all tested conditions.}
    Across 4 model-mode configurations and 4 decoding strategies (8 conditions total), all 1v2 bootstrap CI lower bounds exceed $\theta = 0.60$ and all 2v3 CI upper bounds fall below $\theta$, with permutation $p \leq 0.002$ for all boundary comparisons.
    The most marginal case is Qwen-continuation, where $\text{CI}_\text{lower} = 0.6015$.
    $\Kempirical = 2$ is thus established as a consistent discrimination boundary across all 8 tested conditions at $\leq$1.5B scale, suggesting universality beyond the specific models and decoding strategies studied.
    Higher decoding entropy increases signal strength ($\auc_{1,2}$: $0.69$ greedy $\to$ $0.70$ at $T{=}1.2$) but does not shift the boundary.

  \item \textbf{Cross-model transfer.}
    Classifiers trained on one continuation-mode model and evaluated on another retain 80--92\% of within-model accuracy (Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo: 90--92\%).
    At the 0v1 boundary, cross-model $\auc$ exceeds 0.96 universally.
    Transfer retention of 80--92\% suggests a large text-intrinsic component of the depth signal, rather than generator-specific artifacts.

  \item \textbf{Degradation ordering consistency.}
    Single-feature $\auc$ rankings are highly correlated across continuation-mode models (Spearman $\rho \geq 0.85$), with the same top features---\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std}, \texttt{surp\_d2\_std}---appearing across all three families.
    This shared ordering suggests a common degradation mechanism: each generation step smooths the token-level surprisal landscape.
    A limitation is that depth-pair-level agreement weakens ($\tau \approx 0.37$ at 1v2), indicating that individual feature contributions at the boundary vary across models.

  \item \textbf{Generation mode analysis.}
    Within Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct, rewrite mode yields 1v2 $\auc = 0.6955$ versus continuation's $0.6112$ ($\Delta = +8.4$\,pp), but rewrite-trained classifiers transfer poorly across models (61--63\% retention versus 80--92\% for continuation).
    Cross-mode transfer is asymmetric: continuation$\to$rewrite retains 89\% while rewrite$\to$continuation retains 82\%.
    Continuation mode is therefore recommended as the canonical condition for cross-model comparisons.
\end{enumerate}

\noindent As a secondary contribution, we investigate whether the coarse 3-class ordinal signal implied by $\Kempirical = 2$ enables \emph{graduated filtering}---depth-aware data curation that preserves mildly contaminated text (depth~1, retaining most original signal) while removing deeply corrupted text (depth~$\geq 3$)---and whether such filtering can improve upon binary approaches that discard all synthetic content indiscriminately (Section~\ref{sec:experiments}).

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows.
Section~\ref{sec:related_work} reviews related work.
Section~\ref{sec:method} describes the method.
Section~\ref{sec:experiments} presents experimental results.
Section~\ref{sec:discussion} discusses implications and limitations.
Section~\ref{sec:conclusion} concludes.

93	boundary closer to the detection threshold.
94	
95	The absolute 1v2 $\auc$ varies across models:
96	Qwen-rewrite (0.6955) $>$ Pythia (0.6539) $>$ OLMo (0.6145) $\approx$ Qwen-continuation (0.6112).
97	Notably, the spread due to generation mode within a single model
98	(Qwen-rewrite vs.\ Qwen-continuation: $\Delta = 8.4$\,pp) exceeds the spread
99	across models in the same mode
100	(Pythia vs.\ OLMo: $\Delta = 3.9$\,pp),
101	suggesting that generation protocol is a stronger determinant
102	of detectability than model identity.
103	We examine both factors in Sections~\ref{sec:transfer}
104	and~\ref{sec:generation_mode}.
105	
106	Beyond the $\Kempirical$ boundary, depth discrimination deteriorates
107	rapidly.
108	OLMo shows nonsignificant permutation $p$-values at 3v4
109	($p = 0.064$) and 4v5 ($p = 0.232$), indicating that depth
110	classification beyond generation~2 is indistinguishable from
111	random for this model.
112	Pythia retains marginal effects at these depths
113	($p = 0.006$ and $p = 0.008$, respectively),
114	while Qwen-continuation shows weak but detectable discrimination through
115	3v4 ($p = 0.002$) that fades at 4v5 ($p = 0.006$).
116	
117	%% ====================================================================
118	\subsection{Cross-Model Transfer}
119	\label{sec:transfer}
120	
121	Having established $\Kempirical = 2$ consistently, we next ask: is this boundary a property of the text itself, or an artifact of model self-familiarity?
122	To answer this, we train classifiers on one model's outputs and evaluate on another's.
123	Table~\ref{tab:transfer_matrix} shows the full
124	$4 \times 4$ transfer accuracy matrix for 6-class ordinal depth
125	classification.
126	
127	\begin{table}[t]
128	\centering
129	\small
130	\caption{Cross-model transfer accuracy (6-class ordinal
131	classification).  Diagonal entries (bold): within-model accuracy.
132	Off-diagonal: cross-model transfer.  Retention is computed as
133	off-diagonal accuracy divided by the diagonal entry of the training
134	model.}
135	\label{tab:transfer_matrix}
136	\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
137	\toprule
138	Train $\downarrow$ / Test $\rightarrow$
139	  & Qwen-rw & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-cont \\
140	\midrule
141	Qwen-rw
142	  & \textbf{0.4229} & 0.2590 & 0.2653 & 0.3466 \\
143	Pythia
144	  & 0.2718 & \textbf{0.3856} & 0.3531 & 0.3287 \\
145	OLMo
146	  & 0.2768 & 0.3450 & \textbf{0.3822} & 0.3244 \\
147	Qwen-cont
148	  & 0.3440 & 0.3284 & 0.3112 & \textbf{0.3875} \\
149	\bottomrule
150	\end{tabular}
151	\end{table}
152	
153	\begin{figure}[t]
154	\centering
155	\includegraphics[width=0.85\columnwidth]{figures/fig3_transfer_heatmap.pdf}
156	\caption{Cross-model transfer heatmap (6-class ordinal accuracy).
157	Rows: training model; columns: test model.
158	Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo (both continuation mode) shows high
159	mutual transfer (90--92\% accuracy retention), while Qwen-rewrite
160	transfers poorly to continuation-mode models (61--63\%).

162	\label{fig:transfer_heatmap}
163	\end{figure}
164	
165	Two principal findings emerge (Figure~\ref{fig:transfer_heatmap}).
166	First, transfer between continuation-mode models is high.
167	Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo mutual transfer retains 90--92\% of within-model accuracy
168	(85--86\% retention by Kendall $\tau$).
169	The accuracy-based retention of 90--92\% is complemented by the
170	$\tau$-based retention of 85--86\%, indicating that not only
171	classification accuracy but also the relative depth ordering of
172	predictions is largely preserved.
173	Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$Pythia also transfers well
174	(84--85\% accuracy retention),
175	and Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$OLMo achieves 80--85\%.
176	These retention rates---80--92\% of within-model accuracy preserved across continuation-mode pairs---suggest that a large component of the depth signal is text-intrinsic rather than tied to a specific generator.
177	
178	Second, Qwen-rewrite exhibits catastrophic transfer failure.
179	Classifiers trained on Qwen-rewrite retain only 61--63\% of
180	within-model accuracy when evaluated on Pythia or OLMo
181	(45--50\% by $\tau$).
182	The reverse direction transfers asymmetrically: Pythia/OLMo${\to}$Qwen-rewrite retains 70--72\% of within-model accuracy, higher than the forward 61--63\% but still far below continuation-mode transfer rates (80--92\%).
183	This confirms that rewrite-mode classifiers rely on generation
184	artifacts that do not generalize across models, in contrast
185	to Qwen-continuation, which achieves 80--85\% retention to the same targets.
186	
187	At the 0v1 boundary, cross-model pairwise $\auc$ exceeds 0.96
188	for all model pairs, confirming that the human-vs.-synthetic
189	distinction is universally transferable regardless of generator
190	or mode.
191	The transfer degradation concentrates at deeper boundaries
192	(1v2 and beyond), where model- and mode-specific factors dominate.
193	
194	The aggregate picture is one of modest cross-model loss:
195	mean pairwise $\auc$ is 0.6099 within-model versus 0.5905

198	continuation-mode pairs the within/cross difference narrows

201	%% ====================================================================
202	\subsection{Feature Degradation Ordering}
203	\label{sec:feature_degradation}
204	
205	The transfer results indicate that depth signals are largely text-intrinsic.
206	We next ask what drives discrimination: if the signal is text-intrinsic, different generators should rely on the same features in the same order.

208	independently for each model and comparing them via rank

249	(all $\rho \geq 0.85$).
250	The top-3 features---\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std},
251	and \texttt{surp\_d2\_std}---are shared (up to ordering) across
252	all three continuation-mode configurations
253	(Table~\ref{tab:top_features}).
254	All three measure variability of surprisal or its derivatives,
255	capturing the \emph{heterogeneity} of token-level predictability
256	across the text.
257	That these features degrade in a shared order across generators
258	suggests a common mechanism: each generation step smooths the
259	token-level surprisal landscape, reducing its variance in a
260	model-independent fashion.
261	
262	Qwen-rewrite diverges: its top-ranked feature is
263	\texttt{freq\_entropy}, a lexical diversity measure absent from
264	the continuation-mode top-3 for any model.
265	This corroborates the transfer results in
266	Section~\ref{sec:transfer}---rewrite-mode classifiers learn
267	partly from instruction-following artifacts rather than the

270	Kendall $\tau$ provides a complementary, more conservative
271	perspective:
272	Pythia vs.\ OLMo $\tau = 0.733$,
273	Pythia vs.\ Qwen-continuation $\tau = 0.695$,
274	OLMo vs.\ Qwen-continuation $\tau = 0.543$.

276	Pythia vs.\ Qwen-rewrite $\tau = 0.467$,
277	OLMo vs.\ Qwen-rewrite $\tau = 0.429$.

280	The high Spearman $\rho$ characterizes the \emph{aggregate}
281	feature ranking, but at the depth-pair level the agreement
282	weakens: $\tau \approx 0.37$ at the 1v2 boundary.

284	the relative contribution of individual features at the
285	discrimination boundary---where precision matters most---varies
286	across models.

288	interpretation and a direction for future investigation.
289	
290	%% ====================================================================
291	\subsection{Generation Mode Effect}
292	\label{sec:generation_mode}
293	
294	Finally, we ask whether generation mode---an experimental design choice rather than a text property---affects depth detectability.
295	Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct provides a controlled comparison: rewrite (instruction-based paraphrasing) and continuation (prompt truncation) share the same model weights, as defined in Section~\ref{sec:method}, isolating the effect of generation protocol.
296	
297	Rewrite mode yields higher 1v2 $\auc$ than continuation:
298	0.6955 vs.\ 0.6112, a difference of $+$8.4 percentage points.
299	The advantage persists at 2v3
300	(0.5893 vs.\ 0.5609, $\Delta = +$2.8\,pp)
301	and narrows at 3v4
302	(0.5435 vs.\ 0.5409, $\Delta = +$0.3\,pp),
303	with both modes converging toward chance at deeper levels.
304	The amplified detectability under rewrite mode is consistent
305	with instruction-following introducing systematic deviations
306	from the source text's style---additional artifacts that are
307	discriminable but mode-specific rather than text-intrinsic.
308	
309	Transfer between modes is asymmetric.
310	A classifier trained on Qwen-continuation and evaluated on Qwen-rewrite
311	retains 89\% of within-model accuracy
312	(0.3440 vs.\ 0.3875 diagonal),
313	whereas the reverse direction---Qwen-rewrite trained,
314	Qwen-continuation tested---retains 82\%
315	(0.3466 vs.\ 0.4229 diagonal).
316	The direction of the asymmetry is intuitive:
317	continuation-mode signals form a subset of the information
318	available in rewrite-mode data
319	(which adds instruction-following artifacts on top),
320	so a continuation-trained classifier can partially recognize
321	rewrite-mode outputs but not vice versa.
322	
323	This asymmetry is mirrored in the feature rankings.
324	Qwen-rewrite's top feature (\texttt{freq\_entropy}) is
325	mode-specific and ranks outside the top-3 for every
326	continuation-mode model.
327	Qwen-continuation's top feature (\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}) is shared
328	with Pythia and OLMo, confirming that continuation mode
329	captures primarily text-intrinsic depth signals.
330	
331	The practical implication is a detectability--generalizability
332	tradeoff.
333	Rewrite-mode classifiers achieve higher absolute $\auc$ but
334	transfer poorly across models
335	(Qwen-rewrite$\to$Pythia/OLMo: 61--63\% retention).
336	Continuation-mode classifiers sacrifice 8.4\,pp of within-model
337	$\auc$ but achieve robust cross-model transfer
338	(Qwen-continuation$\to$Pythia: 84--85\%).
339	For deployment scenarios requiring model-agnostic depth
340	estimation, continuation-mode features provide a more reliable
341	foundation despite lower raw discriminability.

\section{Experiments}
\label{sec:experiments}

We evaluate generational depth estimation on four model configurations:
Pythia-1.4B and OLMo-1B in continuation mode, and Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct in both rewrite and continuation modes.
All experiments use the OBD-LightGBM classifier with the 15-dimensional feature set described in Section~\ref{sec:method}.
Each configuration uses a balanced corpus of 5{,}000 texts per depth level (generations 0--5).
We organize results around four questions:
(1)~Does $\Kempirical = 2$ hold across configurations?
(2)~Do depth classifiers transfer across models?
(3)~Is the feature degradation ordering model-independent?
(4)~How does generation mode affect detectability?

%% ====================================================================
\subsection{$\Kempirical = 2$ Across All Configurations}
\label{sec:kstar_boundary}

Table~\ref{tab:kstar_ci} reports pairwise $\auc$ for adjacent depth pairs
across all four configurations, with bootstrap 95\% confidence intervals
(1{,}000 resamples) and permutation-test $p$-values for the critical 1v2
and 2v3 boundaries.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Pairwise $\auc$ for adjacent depth pairs.  Bootstrap 95\% CIs
and permutation $p$-values shown for the $\Kstar$ boundary rows (1v2,
2v3).  $\Kempirical = 2$ requires 1v2 $\text{CI}_\text{low} > \theta$
and 2v3 $\text{CI}_\text{high} < \theta$ with $\theta = 0.60$.
All 0v1 permutation $p \leq 0.002$ (Qwen-continuation 0v1: CI [0.9963, 0.9978], $p = 0.002$).}
\label{tab:kstar_ci}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
 & Qwen-rw & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-cont \\
\midrule
0v1 & 0.9956 & 0.9932 & 0.9970 & 0.9971 \\[4pt]
1v2 & 0.6955 & 0.6539 & 0.6145 & 0.6112 \\
{\footnotesize CI}
  & {\footnotesize [.6859,\,.7041]}
  & {\footnotesize [.6454,\,.6630]}
  & {\footnotesize [.6045,\,.6247]}
  & {\footnotesize [.6015,\,.6213]} \\
{\footnotesize $p$}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002} \\[4pt]
2v3 & 0.5893 & 0.5514 & 0.5496 & 0.5609 \\
{\footnotesize CI}
  & {\footnotesize [.5795,\,.5991]}
  & {\footnotesize [.5417,\,.5628]}
  & {\footnotesize [.5399,\,.5596]}
  & {\footnotesize [.5511,\,.5712]} \\
{\footnotesize $p$}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002}
  & {\footnotesize .002} \\[4pt]
3v4 & 0.5435 & 0.5152 & 0.5091 & 0.5409 \\
4v5 & 0.5340 & 0.5136 & 0.5045 & 0.5141 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

The pattern is uniform across all four configurations:
0v1 discrimination is near-perfect ($\auc > 0.99$),
followed by a sharp drop at 1v2 ($\auc$ range: 0.6112--0.6955),
with 2v3 falling below the decision threshold $\theta = 0.60$
($\auc$ range: 0.5496--0.5893).
All subsequent pairs (3v4, 4v5) converge toward chance.
Figure~\ref{fig:auc_decay} visualizes this decay.

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig2_auc_decay.pdf}
\caption{Pairwise $\auc$ as a function of depth pair across four model-mode configurations (solid) and four decoding strategies (dashed).  All configurations show a sharp drop between 0v1 and 1v2, with 2v3 and deeper pairs falling below the decision threshold $\theta = 0.60$ (horizontal dashed line).  Error bars show bootstrap 95\% CIs for model-mode configurations; decoding strategy curves omit CIs as they were computed on a separate experimental setup.}
\label{fig:auc_decay}
\end{figure}

For the $\Kempirical$ determination, all four 1v2 CI lower bounds exceed
$\theta$: Qwen-rewrite ($\text{CI}_\text{low} = 0.6859$), Pythia (0.6454),
OLMo (0.6045), and Qwen-continuation (0.6015).
Conversely, all four 2v3 CI upper bounds fall below $\theta$:
Qwen-rewrite ($\text{CI}_\text{high} = 0.5991$), Qwen-continuation (0.5712),
Pythia (0.5628), and OLMo (0.5596).
Permutation tests confirm $p = 0.002$ for all eight boundary comparisons.
Together these establish $\Kempirical = 2$ as a consistent discrimination boundary across all tested configurations at $\leq$1.5B scale, suggesting universality beyond the specific models studied.

The most marginal case is Qwen-continuation, where the 1v2 CI lower bound
(0.6015) exceeds $\theta$ by only 0.0015.  This narrow margin
indicates that $\Kempirical = 2$ is robust but not trivially so---continuation-mode
generation produces weaker depth artifacts than rewrite mode, pushing the
boundary closer to the detection threshold.

The absolute 1v2 $\auc$ varies across models:
Qwen-rewrite (0.6955) $>$ Pythia (0.6539) $>$ OLMo (0.6145) $\approx$ Qwen-continuation (0.6112).
Notably, the spread due to generation mode within a single model
(Qwen-rewrite vs.\ Qwen-continuation: $\Delta = 8.4$\,pp) exceeds the spread
across models in the same mode
(Pythia vs.\ OLMo: $\Delta = 3.9$\,pp),
suggesting that generation protocol is a stronger determinant
of detectability than model identity.
We examine both factors in Sections~\ref{sec:transfer}
and~\ref{sec:generation_mode}.

Beyond the $\Kempirical$ boundary, depth discrimination deteriorates
rapidly.
OLMo shows nonsignificant permutation $p$-values at 3v4
($p = 0.064$) and 4v5 ($p = 0.232$), indicating that depth
classification beyond generation~2 is indistinguishable from
random for this model.
Pythia retains marginal effects at these depths
($p = 0.006$ and $p = 0.008$, respectively),
while Qwen-continuation shows weak but detectable discrimination through
3v4 ($p = 0.002$) that fades at 4v5 ($p = 0.006$).

%% ====================================================================
\subsection{Cross-Model Transfer}
\label{sec:transfer}

Having established $\Kempirical = 2$ consistently, we next ask: is this boundary a property of the text itself, or an artifact of model self-familiarity?
To answer this, we train classifiers on one model's outputs and evaluate on another's.
Table~\ref{tab:transfer_matrix} shows the full
$4 \times 4$ transfer accuracy matrix for 6-class ordinal depth
classification.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Cross-model transfer accuracy (6-class ordinal
classification).  Diagonal entries (bold): within-model accuracy.
Off-diagonal: cross-model transfer.  Retention is computed as
off-diagonal accuracy divided by the diagonal entry of the training
model.}
\label{tab:transfer_matrix}
\begin{tabular}{lcccc}
\toprule
Train $\downarrow$ / Test $\rightarrow$
  & Qwen-rw & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-cont \\
\midrule
Qwen-rw
  & \textbf{0.4229} & 0.2590 & 0.2653 & 0.3466 \\
Pythia
  & 0.2718 & \textbf{0.3856} & 0.3531 & 0.3287 \\
OLMo
  & 0.2768 & 0.3450 & \textbf{0.3822} & 0.3244 \\
Qwen-cont
  & 0.3440 & 0.3284 & 0.3112 & \textbf{0.3875} \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\begin{figure}[t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=0.85\columnwidth]{figures/fig3_transfer_heatmap.pdf}
\caption{Cross-model transfer heatmap (6-class ordinal accuracy).
Rows: training model; columns: test model.
Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo (both continuation mode) shows high
mutual transfer (90--92\% accuracy retention), while Qwen-rewrite
transfers poorly to continuation-mode models (61--63\%).
Diagonal entries are within-model baselines.}
\label{fig:transfer_heatmap}
\end{figure}

Two principal findings emerge (Figure~\ref{fig:transfer_heatmap}).
First, transfer between continuation-mode models is high.
Pythia$\leftrightarrow$OLMo mutual transfer retains 90--92\% of within-model accuracy
(85--86\% retention by Kendall $\tau$).
The accuracy-based retention of 90--92\% is complemented by the
$\tau$-based retention of 85--86\%, indicating that not only
classification accuracy but also the relative depth ordering of
predictions is largely preserved.
Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$Pythia also transfers well
(84--85\% accuracy retention),
and Qwen-continuation$\leftrightarrow$OLMo achieves 80--85\%.
These retention rates---80--92\% of within-model accuracy preserved across continuation-mode pairs---suggest that a large component of the depth signal is text-intrinsic rather than tied to a specific generator.

Second, Qwen-rewrite exhibits catastrophic transfer failure.
Classifiers trained on Qwen-rewrite retain only 61--63\% of
within-model accuracy when evaluated on Pythia or OLMo
(45--50\% by $\tau$).
The reverse direction transfers asymmetrically: Pythia/OLMo${\to}$Qwen-rewrite retains 70--72\% of within-model accuracy, higher than the forward 61--63\% but still far below continuation-mode transfer rates (80--92\%).
This confirms that rewrite-mode classifiers rely on generation
artifacts that do not generalize across models, in contrast
to Qwen-continuation, which achieves 80--85\% retention to the same targets.

At the 0v1 boundary, cross-model pairwise $\auc$ exceeds 0.96
for all model pairs, confirming that the human-vs.-synthetic
distinction is universally transferable regardless of generator
or mode.
The transfer degradation concentrates at deeper boundaries
(1v2 and beyond), where model- and mode-specific factors dominate.

The aggregate picture is one of modest cross-model loss:
mean pairwise $\auc$ is 0.6099 within-model versus 0.5905
cross-model.
This gap is driven primarily by Qwen-rewrite; among
continuation-mode pairs the within/cross difference narrows
further.

%% ====================================================================
\subsection{Feature Degradation Ordering}
\label{sec:feature_degradation}

The transfer results indicate that depth signals are largely text-intrinsic.
We next ask what drives discrimination: if the signal is text-intrinsic, different generators should rely on the same features in the same order.
We test this by computing single-feature $\auc$ rankings
independently for each model and comparing them via rank
correlation.

\begin{table}[t]
\centering
\small
\caption{Top-3 features by single-feature $\auc$ ranking for each
model configuration.
Features shared across all three continuation-mode models are in bold.
Qwen-rewrite's top feature (\texttt{freq\_entropy}) is mode-specific.
Spearman $\rho$ (continuation-mode pairs): Pythia--OLMo 0.95,
Pythia--Qwen-continuation 0.9143, OLMo--Qwen-continuation 0.85.}
\label{tab:top_features}
\begin{tabular}{cllll}
\toprule
Rank & Pythia & OLMo & Qwen-rw & Qwen-cont \\
\midrule
1
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}}
  & \texttt{freq\_entropy}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}} \\
2

  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_std}}

  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d2\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}}
  & \textbf{\texttt{surp\_d2\_std}} \\

\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Among continuation-mode models, single-feature $\auc$ rankings

Pythia vs.\ OLMo $\rho = 0.95$,
Pythia vs.\ Qwen-continuation $\rho = 0.9143$,
OLMo vs.\ Qwen-continuation $\rho = 0.85$
(all $\rho \geq 0.85$).
The top-3 features---\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}, \texttt{surp\_std},
and \texttt{surp\_d2\_std}---are shared (up to ordering) across
all three continuation-mode configurations
(Table~\ref{tab:top_features}).
All three measure variability of surprisal or its derivatives,
capturing the \emph{heterogeneity} of token-level predictability
across the text.
That these features degrade in a shared order across generators
suggests a common mechanism: each generation step smooths the
token-level surprisal landscape, reducing its variance in a
model-independent fashion.

Qwen-rewrite diverges: its top-ranked feature is
\texttt{freq\_entropy}, a lexical diversity measure absent from
the continuation-mode top-3 for any model.
This corroborates the transfer results in
Section~\ref{sec:transfer}---rewrite-mode classifiers learn
partly from instruction-following artifacts rather than the
shared surprisal-based signals.

Kendall $\tau$ provides a complementary, more conservative
perspective:
Pythia vs.\ OLMo $\tau = 0.733$,
Pythia vs.\ Qwen-continuation $\tau = 0.695$,
OLMo vs.\ Qwen-continuation $\tau = 0.543$.
Cross-mode correlations are lower:
Pythia vs.\ Qwen-rewrite $\tau = 0.467$,
OLMo vs.\ Qwen-rewrite $\tau = 0.429$.

\paragraph{Limitation.}
The high Spearman $\rho$ characterizes the \emph{aggregate}
feature ranking, but at the depth-pair level the agreement
weakens: $\tau \approx 0.37$ at the 1v2 boundary.
This means that while the overall importance ordering is shared,
the relative contribution of individual features at the
discrimination boundary---where precision matters most---varies
across models.
We view this as a genuine limitation of the text-intrinsic
interpretation and a direction for future investigation.

%% ====================================================================
\subsection{Generation Mode Effect}
\label{sec:generation_mode}

Finally, we ask whether generation mode---an experimental design choice rather than a text property---affects depth detectability.
Qwen2.5-1.5B-Instruct provides a controlled comparison: rewrite (instruction-based paraphrasing) and continuation (prompt truncation) share the same model weights, as defined in Section~\ref{sec:method}, isolating the effect of generation protocol.

Rewrite mode yields higher 1v2 $\auc$ than continuation:
0.6955 vs.\ 0.6112, a difference of $+$8.4 percentage points.
The advantage persists at 2v3
(0.5893 vs.\ 0.5609, $\Delta = +$2.8\,pp)
and narrows at 3v4
(0.5435 vs.\ 0.5409, $\Delta = +$0.3\,pp),
with both modes converging toward chance at deeper levels.
The amplified detectability under rewrite mode is consistent
with instruction-following introducing systematic deviations
from the source text's style---additional artifacts that are
discriminable but mode-specific rather than text-intrinsic.

Transfer between modes is asymmetric.
A classifier trained on Qwen-continuation and evaluated on Qwen-rewrite
retains 89\% of within-model accuracy
(0.3440 vs.\ 0.3875 diagonal),
whereas the reverse direction---Qwen-rewrite trained,
Qwen-continuation tested---retains 82\%
(0.3466 vs.\ 0.4229 diagonal).
The direction of the asymmetry is intuitive:
continuation-mode signals form a subset of the information
available in rewrite-mode data
(which adds instruction-following artifacts on top),
so a continuation-trained classifier can partially recognize
rewrite-mode outputs but not vice versa.

This asymmetry is mirrored in the feature rankings.
Qwen-rewrite's top feature (\texttt{freq\_entropy}) is
mode-specific and ranks outside the top-3 for every
continuation-mode model.
Qwen-continuation's top feature (\texttt{surp\_d1\_std}) is shared
with Pythia and OLMo, confirming that continuation mode
captures primarily text-intrinsic depth signals.

The practical implication is a detectability--generalizability
tradeoff.
Rewrite-mode classifiers achieve higher absolute $\auc$ but

$\auc$ but achieve robust cross-model transfer
(Qwen-continuation$\to$Pythia: 84--85\%).
For deployment scenarios requiring model-agnostic depth
estimation, continuation-mode features provide a more reliable
foundation despite lower raw discriminability.

1	\section{Related Work}
2	\label{sec:related_work}
3	
4	\paragraph{Model Collapse and Recursive Generation.}
5	Training on model-generated data can cause progressive distribution shift known as \emph{model collapse}.
6	Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} showed that iteratively training language models on their own outputs leads to irreversible tail-distribution degradation, with minority modes vanishing across generations.
7	Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} formalized this for self-consuming generative models, proving convergence to a fixed point under mild regularity conditions.
8	Dohmatob et al.~\cite{dohmatob2024model} derived scaling laws for collapse, demonstrating that tail probability mass is lost at rates predictable from model and data scale.
9	Schaeffer et al.~\cite{schaeffer2025position} organized the fragmented literature into a taxonomy of eight definitions across three families.
10	Our $\Kstar$ aligns with their Family~B (distributional deformation), specifically D4 (collapsing variance) and D6 (mode entanglement)---the features that degrade most rapidly in our experiments are precisely variance-based surprisal measures.
11	Kazdan et al.~\cite{kazdan2025collapse} distinguished \emph{replace} and \emph{accumulate} regimes: in the replace regime each generation completely supplants its predecessor, producing faster collapse.
12	Our prompt-chain protocol operates in the replace regime, so $\Kempirical = 2$ is a conservative lower bound; the accumulate regime would yield slower degradation and higher $\Kstar$.
13	Shi et al.~\cite{shi2025generalization} identified a generalization-to-memorization transition in recursively trained models, providing cross-modal evidence that information loss is progressive.
14	These works characterize the macro dynamics of collapse but do not provide tools for per-text generational depth estimation.
15	
16	\paragraph{Binary Synthetic Text Detection.}
17	Distinguishing machine-generated from human-written text is a well-studied binary classification problem.
18	Zellers et al.~\cite{zellers2019grover} demonstrated that the generating model itself is an effective detector, while Ippolito et al.~\cite{ippolito2020detection} analyzed how detection difficulty scales with generation quality.
19	Recent zero-shot methods have narrowed the gap: Mitchell et al.~\cite{mitchell2023detectgpt} introduced DetectGPT, which uses probability curvature to detect machine-generated text without access to the generating model.
20	DivEye~\cite{basani2026diveye} uses surprisal diversity features to detect synthetic text without generator-specific training data, and Min-K\%++~\cite{zhang2024minkpp} adapts membership inference techniques to flag model-generated passages via outlier token likelihoods.
21	CoDeC~\cite{zawalski2026codec} frames contamination detection as in-context learning, calibrating thresholds from few-shot exemplars.
22	
23	All these methods produce binary outputs and do not distinguish generational depth.
24	The connection to membership inference is instructive: Min-K\%++ and related approaches test whether a text appeared in training data---a related but distinct question from how many recursive generation steps it has undergone.
25	A further limitation is that binary detectors cannot separate beneficial recursive generation (e.g., self-refinement, where a model iteratively improves its own output) from harmful recursive contamination, creating systematic false positives when applied to curated synthetic data.
26	Binary features are designed for the human-vs.-synthetic boundary and are not expected to capture fine-grained depth differences, as the distributional shift between adjacent generations is orders of magnitude smaller than the shift between human and first-generation text.
27	
28	\paragraph{Data Selection and Curation.}
29	Principled data selection methods improve training corpus quality through distribution matching and deduplication.
30	DSIR~\cite{xie2023dsir} selects pretraining data by importance resampling against a target distribution.
31	D4~\cite{tirumala2024d4} combines deduplication with diversification to reduce redundancy, and DoReMi~\cite{xie2024doremi} learns domain weights via a proxy model to optimize downstream performance.
32	These methods operate on distributional properties of the corpus but do not estimate whether individual documents have undergone recursive generation.
33	
34	The closest prior work is Drayson et al.~\cite{drayson2025}, who combined binary machine-generated text detection with stratified importance resampling (SIR) to filter synthetic content and prevent model collapse.
35	Their approach is a special case of our graduated filtering framework: when $\Kstar = 1$, ordinal depth estimation reduces to binary classification, and depth-aware curation degenerates to their SIR-based scheme.
36	We generalize this binary formulation to ordinal depth estimation, enabling finer-grained curation that preserves mildly contaminated text (depth~1, retaining most original signal) while removing deeply corrupted text (depth~$\geq 3$).
37	Amin et al.~\cite{amin2025escaping} demonstrated that even weak quality signals suffice to escape model collapse when applied iteratively, suggesting that approximate depth estimates beyond $\Kempirical$ may remain practically useful.
38	Gambetta et al.~\cite{gambetta2025surplexity} proposed surplexity as a text quality metric correlated with generative degradation, though without explicit depth calibration.
39	
40	\paragraph{Watermarking and Provenance.}
41	An alternative approach embeds identifiers at generation time.
42	Kirchenbauer et al.~\cite{kirchenbauer2023watermark} proposed statistical watermarking for LLM outputs by partitioning the vocabulary into green and red token lists conditioned on preceding context.
43	Watermarking is complementary to depth estimation: it requires control over the generation process and cooperation from providers, whereas our method operates post-hoc on unwatermarked text.
44	The two approaches address different threat models---watermarking assumes a cooperative generator, while depth estimation targets uncontrolled settings where provenance metadata is unavailable.

\section{Related Work}
\label{sec:related_work}

\paragraph{Model Collapse and Recursive Generation.}
Training on model-generated data can cause progressive distribution shift known as \emph{model collapse}.
Shumailov et al.~\cite{shumailov2024collapse} showed that iteratively training language models on their own outputs leads to irreversible tail-distribution degradation, with minority modes vanishing across generations.
Alemohammad et al.~\cite{alemohammad2024selfconsuming} formalized this for self-consuming generative models, proving convergence to a fixed point under mild regularity conditions.
Dohmatob et al.~\cite{dohmatob2024model} derived scaling laws for collapse, demonstrating that tail probability mass is lost at rates predictable from model and data scale.
Schaeffer et al.~\cite{schaeffer2025position} organized the fragmented literature into a taxonomy of eight definitions across three families.
Our $\Kstar$ aligns with their Family~B (distributional deformation), specifically D4 (collapsing variance) and D6 (mode entanglement)---the features that degrade most rapidly in our experiments are precisely variance-based surprisal measures.
Kazdan et al.~\cite{kazdan2025collapse} distinguished \emph{replace} and \emph{accumulate} regimes: in the replace regime each generation completely supplants its predecessor, producing faster collapse.
Our prompt-chain protocol operates in the replace regime, so $\Kempirical = 2$ is a conservative lower bound; the accumulate regime would yield slower degradation and higher $\Kstar$.
Shi et al.~\cite{shi2025generalization} identified a generalization-to-memorization transition in recursively trained models, providing cross-modal evidence that information loss is progressive.
These works characterize the macro dynamics of collapse but do not provide tools for per-text generational depth estimation.

\paragraph{Binary Synthetic Text Detection.}
Distinguishing machine-generated from human-written text is a well-studied binary classification problem.
Zellers et al.~\cite{zellers2019grover} demonstrated that the generating model itself is an effective detector, while Ippolito et al.~\cite{ippolito2020detection} analyzed how detection difficulty scales with generation quality.
Recent zero-shot methods have narrowed the gap: Mitchell et al.~\cite{mitchell2023detectgpt} introduced DetectGPT, which uses probability curvature to detect machine-generated text without access to the generating model.
DivEye~\cite{basani2026diveye} uses surprisal diversity features to detect synthetic text without generator-specific training data, and Min-K\%++~\cite{zhang2024minkpp} adapts membership inference techniques to flag model-generated passages via outlier token likelihoods.
CoDeC~\cite{zawalski2026codec} frames contamination detection as in-context learning, calibrating thresholds from few-shot exemplars.

All these methods produce binary outputs and do not distinguish generational depth.
The connection to membership inference is instructive: Min-K\%++ and related approaches test whether a text appeared in training data---a related but distinct question from how many recursive generation steps it has undergone.
A further limitation is that binary detectors cannot separate beneficial recursive generation (e.g., self-refinement, where a model iteratively improves its own output) from harmful recursive contamination, creating systematic false positives when applied to curated synthetic data.
Binary features are designed for the human-vs.-synthetic boundary and are not expected to capture fine-grained depth differences, as the distributional shift between adjacent generations is orders of magnitude smaller than the shift between human and first-generation text.

\paragraph{Data Selection and Curation.}
Principled data selection methods improve training corpus quality through distribution matching and deduplication.
DSIR~\cite{xie2023dsir} selects pretraining data by importance resampling against a target distribution.
D4~\cite{tirumala2024d4} combines deduplication with diversification to reduce redundancy, and DoReMi~\cite{xie2024doremi} learns domain weights via a proxy model to optimize downstream performance.
These methods operate on distributional properties of the corpus but do not estimate whether individual documents have undergone recursive generation.

The closest prior work is Drayson et al.~\cite{drayson2025}, who combined binary machine-generated text detection with stratified importance resampling (SIR) to filter synthetic content and prevent model collapse.
Their approach is a special case of our graduated filtering framework: when $\Kstar = 1$, ordinal depth estimation reduces to binary classification, and depth-aware curation degenerates to their SIR-based scheme.
We generalize this binary formulation to ordinal depth estimation, enabling finer-grained curation that preserves mildly contaminated text (depth~1, retaining most original signal) while removing deeply corrupted text (depth~$\geq 3$).
Amin et al.~\cite{amin2025escaping} demonstrated that even weak quality signals suffice to escape model collapse when applied iteratively, suggesting that approximate depth estimates beyond $\Kempirical$ may remain practically useful.
Gambetta et al.~\cite{gambetta2025surplexity} proposed surplexity as a text quality metric correlated with generative degradation, though without explicit depth calibration.

\paragraph{Watermarking and Provenance.}
An alternative approach embeds identifiers at generation time.
Kirchenbauer et al.~\cite{kirchenbauer2023watermark} proposed statistical watermarking for LLM outputs by partitioning the vocabulary into green and red token lists conditioned on preceding context.
Watermarking is complementary to depth estimation: it requires control over the generation process and cooperation from providers, whereas our method operates post-hoc on unwatermarked text.
